Readings · in your frame

Notes on the board

What is calculated, and what is drawn.

Times are in seconds and distances in light-seconds (ls), so light moves 1 ls per second and every light ray in the diagram climbs at 45°. Speeds are fractions of the speed of light, c. Every position, time and clock reading comes from the Lorentz transformation between the platform and the frame you ride with.

t′ = γ (t − v x), x′ = γ (x − v t), γ = 1/√(1 − v²)

The board

The top strip is everything at one moment of your time: the rails and platform clocks belong to the platform; each train carries its own clocks, synchronised in its own frame. Below, the spacetime diagram shows the whole history, distance across and your time up; the dashed orange line is now, the moment shown in the strip.

Clocks, lengths and “now”

Seen from another frame, a moving train’s clocks run slow by γ and are out of step along its length: the front clock lags the back one by v L₀. A moving train is shorter by γ, because measuring a length means marking both ends at the same moment, and “the same moment” differs between frames; the dashed coloured lines are each train’s own “now”.

Invariants

The interval s² = Δt² − Δx² between two events is the same in every frame. The dotted curves t² − x² = constant do not move when you change frames; everything else slides along them.

Hands and keys

Click a train, traveller, tunnel or event to select it; drag events in the diagram, drag trains and tunnels along the track, and drag a train’s round handle in the diagram to change its speed. Drag empty diagram to pan. Space pause · F next frame · Delete removes · 1–7 plates.

Drawn for clarity: train heights, clock faces and the speed of play. Trains are rigid and move in straight lines (the traveller’s turn is instant); what is shown is what each frame measures, not what a camera would see, since light takes time to reach an eye.

Further reading: Taylor & Wheeler, Spacetime Physics · Feynman Lectures, Volume I, chapter 15
